titulo: New Zealand Recognizes a Mountain as a Legal Person

fuente.licencia: Dominio público (VOA, gobierno de EE. UU.)
fuente.nota: Text shortened by paragraphs; sentences unchanged.

parrafos: The mountain is now known by its Māori name, Taranaki Maunga. The Māori people of New Zealand represent about 15 percent of the country’s population.
Taranaki Maunga is a dormant volcano on New Zealand’s North Island. Snow covers the top of the 2,516-meter-high mountain. It is a popular place for tourism, hiking and snow sports.

The legal recognition of the mountain is one of the steps New Zealand’s government has taken to make up for harm the indigenous population suffered in the past. The new law makes it known that the Taranaki area was stolen from the Māori after New Zealand was colonized.

The new law gives Taranaki Maunga all the rights, powers, duties, responsibilities and liabilities of a person. The law says a newly created group will be “the face and voice” of the mountain. Four members from local Māori tribes and four members appointed by the country's conservation minister will be in the group.

Paul Goldsmith is the lawmaker responsible for the legal settlements between the government and Māori tribes. In a speech to Parliament, he said, “The mountain has long been an honored ancestor, a source of physical, cultural and spiritual sustenance and a final resting place."

In 1840, Māori tribes and representatives of the British government signed the Treaty of Waitangi. The treaty promised the Māori would keep the rights to their land and resources. However, the British government began breaking parts of the treaty after that.

In 1865, the government took a large area of Taranaki land, including the mountain, to punish the Māori for rebelling against British rule. Over the next one hundred years, hunting and sports groups helped oversee how the land was used, but the Māori did not.
Goldsmith told the Associated Press that, in the past, Māori customs connected to the mountain were banned while the government supported tourism in the area.

The Māori protest movement of the 1970s and 1980s led to increased recognition of the Māori language, culture and rights in New Zealand’s law. This has included billions of dollars to pay for the harm caused by breaking the Treaty of Waitangi.

The mountain's legal rights are in place to support its health and wellbeing. The law will support traditional uses of the land and calls for conservation work to protect the native wildlife. The mountain will remain open to the public.

New Zealand was the first country in the world to recognize landforms as people. In 2014, a law gave personhood to Te Urewera, a large forest on the North Island. Government ownership ended and the Tūhoe tribe became its guardian.

All 123 lawmakers in Parliament supported the new law for Taranaki Maunga. The unity of the vote was a change from recent disagreements in New Zealand about proposed changes to the Treaty of Waitangi itself.

In November, about 40,000 people marched to Parliament to protest a new law with proposed changes to the treaty. The protesters said the new law would take away Māori rights and harm the progress that has been made during the last 50 years.
titulo_es: New Zealand recognises a mountain as a legal person
resumen_es: New Zealand grants legal personhood to Mount Taranaki Maunga as redress to the Māori people, against the background of the history of the Treaty of Waitangi and other similar recognitions.
nivel_motivo: The legal vocabulary (liabilities, settlements, personhood) raises the measured level, but the sentences are short and the content is very clear: B2.

ideas_clave.idea: A dormant volcano on the North Island, popular with tourists, is now officially called by its Māori name, Taranaki Maunga.
Granting the mountain legal status is part of the government's effort to compensate the Māori for land taken from them after colonisation.
The law gives the mountain the full rights and obligations of a person, represented by a body made up equally of Māori and ministerial appointees.
The minister in charge describes the mountain as a revered ancestor and a source of physical, cultural and spiritual nourishment.
Although the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi guaranteed Māori land rights, the British broke it, confiscating the area in 1865 and later banning Māori customs linked to the mountain.
Māori protests in the 1970s and 1980s led to greater legal recognition and large compensation payments.
The new status aims to protect the mountain's wellbeing and wildlife while keeping it open to visitors.
New Zealand pioneered this approach in 2014 by giving legal personhood to the Te Urewera forest.
The law passed unanimously, in contrast with recent strong disputes and mass protests over a proposal to amend the treaty itself.

resumen_modelo: The text reports that New Zealand has granted legal personhood to a dormant volcano on its North Island, now officially known by its Māori name, Taranaki Maunga. This measure forms part of the government's efforts to redress the injustices suffered by the indigenous population, as the law acknowledges that the area was stolen from the Māori following colonisation. From now on, the mountain enjoys all the rights and obligations of a person, and a body composed of four Māori representatives and four members appointed by the conservation minister will speak on its behalf. Historically, the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi had promised the Māori control of their land, yet the British soon disregarded it: in 1865 the land was confiscated as a punishment for rebellion, and Māori customs were later banned. Only after the protest movements of the 1970s and 1980s did Māori rights gain recognition and substantial compensation. The new law seeks to protect the mountain's health and wildlife while keeping it accessible to the public. New Zealand had already been a pioneer in 2014 with the Te Urewera forest. Finally, the law was approved unanimously, in sharp contrast with the recent controversy over proposed changes to the treaty.
